blocks.t: These terms govern your use of the cypherpunk_vpn software and, where applicable, your participation in the project's community and mesh. Because cypherpunk_vpn is free software rather than a service, most of the conventional terms (subscription, billing, refunds, support) do not apply; the terms that do apply are shorter and more honest than the commercial alternative. The companion PRIVACY_NOTICE.md covers data; this document covers software, contributions and dispute.

cypherpunk_vpn is free software published under AGPL-3.0-or-later with a dual-license commercial path. The maintainer publishes the source; the maintainer does not operate a VPN service. When you run cypherpunk_vpn, you are operating your own VPN using the project's code. You are responsible for:
the infrastructure you run it on (cloud accounts, hardware tokens, exit nodes, network egress);
the laws of the jurisdictions in which your infrastructure sits (path-selection design makes this a first-class concern);
the traffic that leaves your exit (see the threat model for what an exit operator can see);
the costs you incur (cover-traffic bandwidth, hardware tokens, cloud bills — FUNDING.md records the maintainer's standing on costs).

There is no subscription, no automatic renewal, no billing cycle, no refund policy and no support contract. If you contributed funding voluntarily, that contribution is governed by FUNDING.md and is not a purchase.

The SECURITY.md file honestly states what this release does and does not protect against. Of particular note:
The traffic-analysis defenses are measured against published attacks but are not independent evaluations; residual leakage is documented in WF_REAL_RERUN3.md.
A free-tier server stops forwarding when its monthly cap is reached (FEE_GUARD.md); Fly.io has no hard spending limit.
No hardware attestation is implemented; the descriptor attestation roadmap is in ROADMAP.md.
One owner running every hop can correlate the chain end to end; more hops under one operator are not anonymity from that operator.
The cloak's server authentication is the project's composition, with regression and mutation tests but not an independent review.
Endpoint root/host memory inspection is outside the protection boundary.

The conventional commercial VPN terms of service — like OVPN's or NordVPN's or ExpressVPN's — typically run to thousands of words covering subscription, billing, automatic renewal, refund policy, mandatory binding arbitration with a class-action waiver, indemnification, export controls and limitation of liability. Those terms exist because those products are paid services with a customer relationship.

This notice covers the cypherpunk_vpn project and the software it publishes. The project is free software under AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a commercial dual-licensing path. It is not a service. There is no account, no payment, no support contract and no central operator, so the project holds no data about the people who run it. That follows from how the software is built, not from a promise. The parties who do see parts of your traffic are listed in section 5.

The project is maintained under the pseudonym R1VER77. There is no company, no paid staff and no support desk. If a legal entity is ever formed, its jurisdiction will be named here, and the reason recorded in DECISIONS.md. Today there is none.
If you run the software, you operate your own tunnel with the project's code. People who use your deployment should read your notice, not this one.

Nothing. There is no account system, sign-up, email list, payment, telemetry, error reporting or analytics. The project's website is its repository. GitHub's own privacy policy covers issues, pull requests and their notifications.
The commit history is public and signed with hardware-backed SSH keys (SIGNED_REPOSITORY.md).

sections.heading: 3. What the software does not keep

blocks.t: No record of your browsing on the servers.
The relay and exit services send their output to nowhere (StandardOutput=null, LogLevelMax=emerg in deploy/cypherpunk-vpn*.service).
Their working state lives in RAM.
The exit's DNS resolver runs with query logging off (tools/exit_resolver.py).
On a Fly.io exit, deploy/fly/init.sh prints nothing, because a Machine's output goes to Fly's log store.
The managed validation checks that a chain leaves no retained data behind (MANAGED_VALIDATION.md, multi-hop evidence).

One counter per server. To keep a free-tier server under its monthly cap, each server stores how many bytes it has sent this month, rounded to 16 MiB (FEE_GUARD.md). It is one total per server: no clients, no destinations, no times.

No connection records. While you are connected, the servers hold their current peer's address in memory, as any tunnel must. They do not write it down. Cloud providers can still see addresses on their own network (section 5).
No device or advertising identifiers. The build contains no analytics or telemetry SDK. third_party/SOURCES.json lists every vendored upstream.
No DNS history. The client's signed local blocklist answers blocked names inside the tunnel. The exit's recursive resolver keeps no per-client queries.
No payment data. There is no payment system. FUNDING.md records any funding the project receives; at present there is none.

sections.heading: 4. What the software handles on your own devices

blocks.t: Settings and enrollment.
On the client, the signed chain profile you enrolled lives in /etc/cypherpunk-vpn/enrolled.
On the operator's machine, the chains and the cloud server records live in ~/.config/cypherpunk-vpn/.
They name your servers and providers, not you.
Keys.
Keys are made on the device that uses them, in a vault at /etc/cypherpunk-vpn/vault.
The vault is sealed to a security key (FIDO2 hmac-secret) or a TPM where available (HARDWARE_BOUND_SESSIONS.md).
Private keys stay on the device. The device request you hand to the operator carries only public keys.
Running state. Status files and PIDs are kept in RAM (tmpfs) and disappear when the service stops or the machine restarts.
Diagnostics. cypherpunk status, cypherpunk doctor and the desktop app show connection details to you. Running them sends nothing anywhere.
The design limits what each party learns, but none of them learns nothing. See also the threat model.

Your ISP or local network. Can see: That you send encrypted traffic to one address (your first server, or your upstream VPN); its timing and volume. Cannot see: What is inside it. The carrier is designed to look like HTTP/3 or HTTPS; that disguise has not been independently evaluated.

Your first server's provider (AWS, Oracle, Azure, …). Can see: The address you connect from, the address of the next server, and the timing and volume of the traffic. Cannot see: The contents, which are encrypted with hybrid post-quantum key exchange.
Each server along the chain. Can see: Only the server before it and the server after it. Cannot see: Your address (except the first server), the destination, and the contents.
The exit (yours, or a mesh peer's). Can see: The traffic leaving the tunnel and where it goes; DNS queries reach its resolver. Cannot see: Your address. It sees only the server before it.
The exit's provider. Can see: The same as the exit. On Fly.io, the exit's outgoing address is shared with other Fly customers and can change (FLY_EXIT.md). Cannot see: Your address.
Every cloud provider you use. Can see: Who holds the account and what calls are made to its API. Cannot see: What other providers see.
Websites. Can see: The exit's address and what you send them. Cannot see: Your address.
The I2P network (with --front i2p). Can see: That you take part in I2P. Cannot see: Your address, and that the destination is a VPN server.
Your security key's maker. Can see: Nothing about your VPN use. Cannot see: The sealed secrets.
GitHub. Can see: Whatever you post in an issue or pull request. Cannot see: Anything about your deployment.
One operator who runs every server in a chain can link its ends. Adding hops under that same operator does not change this.

There is no operating entity, so there is no entity jurisdiction. The law where your servers run applies to the data on them. The project leaves that choice to you; SUPPORT_MATRIX.md lists what works where.

An order served on the maintainer personally is governed by the law that applies to the maintainer, not by the project. The project's defence is structural: the logs, account database and payment records such an order would ask for do not exist.
The project holds no personal data about you, so there is nothing to access, correct, delete or move under GDPR or CCPA. Under AGPL-3.0-or-later you can do more:
read, audit and change the source (CONTRIBUTING.md);
run it entirely on your own infrastructure;
rerun the evidence yourself (the validation tools in tools/ and the formal models in formal/);
fork it. If you run a modified version as a network service, AGPL §13 requires you to offer that version's source.
The software is not aimed at children and collects nothing from anyone of any age.
This notice changes only by signed commit, and material changes are noted in the CHANGELOG. The file's git history is its version record.
Open an issue on the repository. There is no email address, support desk or chat channel. Report security problems privately, as described in SECURITY.md.
